sections: The market is severely underestimating Micron Technology's intrinsic value. Given HBM's inherent wafer penalty and the ongoing price recovery in HBM, the near-total absence of new HBM entrants (the barriers to entry are extremely high), AI-driven demand for DRAM and NAND that keeps rising while effective supply additions remain absent before 2028 (i.e., a supply–demand imbalance beyond anything seen in past cycles), Strategic Customer Agreements (SCAs) that raise Micron's earnings floor, and Micron's product-mix optimization (with the share of data-center-related revenue rising sharply) — I believe Micron's target price should be $1,400 (a valuation based on 12x Micron's net income, projected one year beyond FY2026 Q4).

1. HBM inherently carries a wafer penalty: producing the same number of bits in HBM consumes roughly four times as many wafers as conventional DRAM. I won't go deep into the technical reasons (advanced packaging, through-silicon via (TSV), thermal management, chemical materials, stacking process, and so on). HBM is a direct cause of this storage shortage — arguably the root cause, since HBM is exactly what AI data centers are short of most, meaning the most direct increment of structural demand comes from HBM. Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix have all tilted more resources toward HBM, which has pushed wafer consumption far above historical levels. Combined with AI data centers' seemingly endless appetite for HBM, this has produced the current storage supercycle (starting from HBM, then spreading to DRAM, then to NAND and HDD).

My own caveat: the structural problem on the supply side will eventually get solved. A structural change on the supply side can only temporarily extend the cycle — it can't eliminate it. To truly extend or even eliminate the cycle, you need a structural change on the demand side. And to be fair, that structural change in demand does appear to be happening.

2. No new entrant will show up in HBM for the next several years, including CXMT. The technical barriers are so high that Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix have a firm lock on this slice of the pie, which means the root cause of the storage supply shortage — HBM — can only be addressed by these three players. So in theory, as long as these three maintain a degree of supply discipline, or as long as technological progress doesn't solve the HBM wafer-penalty problem too quickly, this AI storage supercycle could persist until the three players bring HBM's wafer penalty down to a level that resolves the supply–demand balance.

My own caveat: the supply side can't be counted on here either. Under the pull of high margins, HBM yield problems are bound to improve substantially — or at least improve to some degree — and that improvement would likely ease the supply–demand tightness and push spot prices down. That said, the prevailing market view right now is that HBM yield ramp will remain a bottleneck, since HBM4E and HBM5 will only get harder.

3. HBM demand is enormous, and possibly larger than the market currently imagines. The consensus among multiple investment banks is that the HBM market will break $100B in 2027 and could reach $150–200B in 2028. If this consensus is correct, and assuming Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix hold their current HBM market shares, Micron would earn $20B in HBM revenue in 2027 and $30–40B in 2028 (a more conservative estimate would put Micron's HBM revenue at $15B in 2027 and $20–25B in 2028 — I lean toward the more optimistic scenario). Also, per the latest authoritative data, HBM's per-bit margin is currently lower than conventional DRAM's, which is abnormal in a market-driven environment — under conditions where everything is in shortage, the harder-to-make product should obviously cost more. The market expects HBM's per-bit price could double by 2027 (this is already baked into the TAM figures above). As HBM margins rise, Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix will only keep tilting more resources toward HBM (see the roughly $950B in "letters of intent" that Samsung and SK hynix signed with U.S. tech giants in July). Tilting more capacity toward HBM will simply keep pushing conventional DRAM and NAND prices higher.

My own caveat: the rate of price increase (the second derivative) for DRAM and NAND is expected to slow sharply by 2026 Q3, because consumer-electronics price hikes are already near their limit — pushing prices further would trigger demand destruction in consumer electronics.

Even so, this should keep revenue and net income growing (note: Micron is expected to maintain roughly 20% supply growth through 2026–2027). [In its latest earnings report, Micron said it has already booked $1B in HBM4 revenue, and that HBM4 is ramping to mature production meaningfully faster than HBM3E did — meaning its HBM4 revenue ramp should be quite steep.]

4. AI's ever-rising demand for DRAM and NAND, combined with far-too-small supply additions, is extending the cycle. SK hynix's leadership believes this storage supercycle will last at least through 2030 (this is their view, not mine). The current shortage is indeed still deepening, and 2027 is set to be the worst year (market consensus); even by 2028, the supply–demand picture is only expected to ease slightly from a state of outright shortage — and this, in fact, is where the market has a big disagreement right now.

Looking at Micron's own financials: the Cloud Memory Business Unit (CMBU) plus Core Data Center Business Unit (CDBU) — i.e., data-center-related businesses — now account for 60% of combined revenue. CMBU grew 78% QoQ and CDBU grew 103% QoQ, the two fastest-growing of Micron's four business units, and both are likely to keep growing at a rapid clip (enterprise SSD revenue alone has already reached $5B a quarter and is doubling; Micron also disclosed that NAND prices rose more than 80% that quarter, ahead of DRAM's 60%-plus increase).

The most worrying segment is the Mobile and Client Business Unit (MCBU), since consumer-electronics price hikes are already close to their ceiling — but MCBU accounts for only 28% of revenue and that share is likely to keep shrinking. The pleasant surprise is the Automotive and Embedded Business Unit (AEBU), i.e., automotive and robotics: management says L2-level driver-assist vehicles use 5x the storage of a typical car, that the penetration rate of L2-level vehicles will double this year (reaching 20%), then double again by 2030 (reaching 40%), and that a single robot needs 10x the storage of an L2-level vehicle.

AEBU currently accounts for only 11% of Micron's total revenue. Under management's assumptions, this segment's revenue could rise from today's $4.6B per quarter to $12B per quarter three years out (accounting for possible delays in robot volume ramp and possible declines in storage prices) — a staggering number. On my own rough estimate, three years from now AEBU revenue could catch up to, and even fully surpass, consumer-electronics revenue.

5. SCAs raise the floor on Micron's profitability. Micron has signed 16 SCAs to date; 14 of them together commit to cumulative minimum revenue of $100B, backed by $22B in customer cash deposits, covering 20% of DRAM and 33% of NAND volumes. These contracts set a floor price and a ceiling price (the ceiling is pegged to 2026 Q2 spot prices, while the floor is set above the peak of any past cycle — I'll roughly assume the floor implies a gross margin of 70–75%).

It's worth thinking about this alongside SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM), since the floor-guarantee mechanism is the same idea. Based on a rough calculation (assuming Micron's current 85% gross margin, no step-change in capex, and a weighted-average contract term of 4 years), the default risk on these SCAs is low: customers would only have an incentive to default if spot prices fell 40% below the contract floor, and would only have an incentive to renegotiate if prices fell more than 50% (assuming these contracts run through 2028). Under current conditions, a 50%-plus spot price decline looks unlikely, but if it happened, it would genuinely hurt Micron's revenue and net income.

[Working backward from statements by SanDisk management: the mainstream market forecast is that AI-related NAND demand will be 400EB in 2026, about 30% of total NAND demand, and 610EB in 2027, about 40% of total NAND demand. SanDisk management expects global enterprise SSD demand to reach 1.2ZB by 2030, which lines up with the current mainstream market forecast. On this trajectory, total storage demand would roughly triple between 2026 and 2030 — yet SK hynix management has explicitly said its own expansion plan only doubles capacity by 2030. That gap suggests the shortage could genuinely persist past 2028.]

Micron management's goal is to eventually put more than half of its bit shipments or revenue under the SCA framework (this is standard practice across storage companies right now). I find this highly credible and achievable (compare to SanDisk's own targets of 50% NBM coverage by 2027 and 67% by 2028), and I think Micron management will likely hit a similar milestone by 2028 (this needs to be tracked going forward).

Assume Micron locks in SCA coverage of 50% of DRAM and 67% of NAND by 2028. That would put Micron's guaranteed SCA revenue floor at roughly $250–350B (accounting for continued spot price increases, especially HBM repricing), with a weighted-average contract term of 4 years (today's industry standard). That implies a minimum annual revenue floor of roughly $75B going forward — and even if spot prices fell 50%, revenue would still be around $70B (since we estimate customers would only have default incentive once spot prices fall more than 40%). Based on current data, Micron's FY2026 Q4 revenue is projected at $50B, and FY2027 revenue will likely exceed $300B — [this only requires 15% shipment growth and 30% spot price growth] — of which spot-market revenue would be roughly $150B.

In the market's most pessimistic scenario for 2028 (the year when risks concentrate and are released), Micron would likely still post around $150B in revenue, while holding gross margin near 75% and net margin near 60% (i.e., $90B in net income). And as storage demand keeps rising into 2029, along with higher shipment volumes (assuming prices hold at 2028 levels), Micron should be able to earn at least $100B in net income.

As long as AI's structural demand holds up, $100B in net income is close to Micron's earnings floor — or at least close to it. If Micron can sustain $100B in net income, its valuation multiple could very plausibly get rerated. Applying a 15x P/E to 2028 net income would put Micron's valuation around $1.5T, implying a share price of $1,300.

Micron management has also said that starting later this year, it will return excess cash to shareholders. Factoring in buybacks would push the target price even higher (Micron's most recent quarterly free cash flow was $18B; extrapolating from the FY2027 revenue estimate, Micron's 2027 free cash flow could reach a staggering $150B, and cumulative free cash flow over the following two years could exceed $200B). Accounting for WACC, though, the share-price uplift from buybacks is roughly offset by the discount rate, so I'm keeping the target price at $1,300.

[Note: all of this assumes spot prices fall 50% by 2028. Anything more optimistic than that scenario pushes the target price above $1,300. I plan to build a model to test this going forward.]

• ☐Whether HBM capacity keeps getting sold out well ahead of time (as of now, capacity through 2027 is already fully allocated, even for DRAM)
  • ☐Whether DRAM and NAND contract prices start declining ahead of schedule rather than rising (or rise less than the market expects)
  • ☐Whether HBM yield improves substantially (i.e., the wafer penalty declines sooner than expected)
  • ☐Whether Micron rigorously executes management's plan to raise SCA coverage and customer collateral
  • ☐Whether CXMT's capacity expansion causes consumer-grade DRAM to become saturated earlier than expected, ending the price rally prematurely
  • ☐Whether new fab output (wafer starts) from Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix comes online earlier than expected
  • ☐Whether HBM pricing gets revised again
  • ☐Whether the top-five hyperscalers maintain their capex growth rate (this is the upstream variable driving HBM demand)
  • ☐Whether CXMT's DRAM products catch up to Samsung and SK hynix's mainstream specs of the same generation before 2027 (threshold: third-party benchmarks or customer qualification show speed and yield gaps below 5%)

If any of the following happens, I'll admit I was wrong:

  1. NAND and DRAM contract prices hit an inflection point earlier than the market expects (this also counts if price gains simply fall short of market expectations sooner than expected)
  2. HBM contract prices fail to rise meaningfully, and per-bit margin remains below conventional DRAM's
  3. CXMT's capacity expansion runs far ahead of market expectations (the biggest price gains right now are coming from conventional DRAM; if CXMT's rapid expansion causes conventional DRAM prices to collapse early, Micron's revenue and net income would take a real hit)
  4. Micron fails to execute its stated strategy of raising SCA coverage and customer collateral, or fails to keep growing its revenue share outside consumer electronics
  5. New fab output (wafer starts) comes online earlier than expected
  6. The top-five hyperscalers' capex growth falls short of expectations
  7. CXMT's DRAM products catch up to Samsung's and SK hynix's mainstream specs of the same generation before 2027

What the market thinks: Micron is a classic cyclical stock.

Where I differ: HBM's degree of customization greatly weakens its cyclical character. At the same time, HBM's unavoidable physical wafer penalty, combined with AI's enormous demand, could sustain a long-lasting supply–demand imbalance this cycle. That imbalance is in turn driving the signing of long-term agreements (LTAs), which raise the floor on Micron's earnings. Meanwhile, entirely new demand from humanoid robots and autonomous driving should bring substantial incremental revenue, offsetting the risk that consumer-electronics price increases are peaking.
